ety.text: From Middle English gulf, goulf, golf, from Old French golf, from Italian golfo, from Late Latin colfos, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos, “bosom, gulf”), of obscure origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kʷelp- (“to curve, arch”).

senses.d: A hollow place in the earth; an abyss; a deep chasm or basin.
ex: He then surveyed / Hell and the gulf between.
Witch's mummy, maw and gulf / Of the ravined salt sea shark,

senses.d: That which swallows irretrievably; a whirlpool; a sucking eddy.
ex: [T]here is no such mine, / None; but a gulf of ruin, swallowing gold, not making.

senses.d: A portion of an ocean or sea extending into the land; a partially landlocked sea
A large deposit of ore in a lode.
A wide interval or gap; a separating space.
ex: Between us and you there is a great gulf fixed.
`Behold now, let the Dead and Living meet! Across the gulf of Time they still are one.'

senses.d: A difference, especially a large difference, between groups.
ex: The result is a widening gulf between people’s reality and what they are relentlessly told they actually believe in and care about.

senses.d: The bottom part of a list of those awarded a degree, for those who have only just passed.
To award a degree to somebody who has only just passed sufficiently.
ex: The mention of gulfed and plucked men brings me back to myself.
The good Professor scolded, predicted that they would all be either gulfed or ploughed.

ety.text: Borrowed from Italian golfo, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, culfus, alteration of colpus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos). Doublet of gouffre.
From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, colphus, culfus, alteration of colpus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos). Doublet of colpo.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, colphus, culfus, alteration of colpus following hypercorrection of the popular pronunciation of Latin 'ph' as 'p', itself from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos).
